---
title: "Coding a categorical predictor"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---

A categorical predictor has labels rather than intrinsic numerical distances. **Contrast coding** constructs numeric design columns that make declared comparisons estimable.

Changing the coding changes coefficient coordinates while preserving fitted values and hence the [residuals](residuals.qmd), which are observed minus fitted responses, for an unchanged model space.

With nouns as the reference, the MALD design columns make each remaining coefficient a comparison with fitted noun latency. Reconstructing all three category means will verify that the coordinates changed while the fitted values did not.

Why do we need coding at all? A numerical predictor already tells us what multiplication to perform. The labels *noun*, *verb*, and *adjective* do not. Assigning the arbitrary numbers $1$, $2$, and $3$ would impose an order and equal spacing that the labels themselves do not contain. Contrast coding instead creates columns whose entries are chosen to represent particular comparisons.

## Treatment coding in MALD

We restrict the analysis to the three largest lexical part-of-speech classes in the MALD regression: noun, verb, and adjective. MALD's part-of-speech field summarizes word forms in SUBTLEX; the prepared data contain no token annotations from sentential contexts.

The restriction is data driven and descriptive. MALD contains additional lexical categories, while these three have the largest representation in the prepared item data. The [MALD measurements](multiple-regression.qmd#mald-word-item-data) explain how the item summary was constructed.

With noun as the reference, treatment coding uses

$$
\begin{array}{c|cc}
&V&A\\\hline
\text{noun}&0&0\\
\text{verb}&1&0\\
\text{adjective}&0&1
\end{array}.
$$

The fitted mean is

$$
\mu_i
=
\beta_0+\beta_VV_i+\beta_AA_i
+\beta_fF_i^c+\beta_dD_i^c+\beta_pP_i^c.
$$

At the centered numeric predictors, $\beta_0$ is the fitted noun mean, $\beta_V$ is the verb-minus-noun contrast, and $\beta_A$ is the adjective-minus-noun contrast.

Substitution verifies these meanings. A noun row has $V_i=0$ and $A_i=0$, so the category part of its fitted value is $\beta_0$. A verb row has $V_i=1$ and $A_i=0$, giving $\beta_0+\beta_V$. Subtracting the noun prediction leaves $\beta_V$. The coefficient meaning follows from the two rows of numbers, rather than from the software label attached to the coefficient.

Multiplying a coding row by the category coefficients makes the comparison explicit:

$$
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{noun}&\beta_0+0\beta_V+0\beta_A\\
\text{verb}&\beta_0+1\beta_V+0\beta_A\\
\text{adjective}&\beta_0+0\beta_V+1\beta_A
\end{array}.
$$

```{r}
#| label: fit-mald-treatment-coding
library(ggplot2)

mald <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-items.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
mald$log_frequency_c <-
  mald$log_frequency_subtlex - mean(mald$log_frequency_subtlex)
mald$log_duration_c <- mald$log_duration - mean(mald$log_duration)
mald$n_phones_c <- mald$n_phones - mean(mald$n_phones)

major_pos <- subset(
  mald,
  part_of_speech %in% c("Noun", "Verb", "Adjective")
)
major_pos$part_of_speech <- factor(
  major_pos$part_of_speech,
  levels = c("Noun", "Verb", "Adjective")
)
contrasts(major_pos$part_of_speech) <- contr.treatment(3)

fit <- lm(
  mean_log_rt ~ part_of_speech + log_frequency_c +
    log_duration_c + n_phones_c,
  data = major_pos
)

contrasts(major_pos$part_of_speech)
coef(summary(fit))
```

The following actual rows show the word-form labels being encoded:

```{r}
#| label: inspect-mald-pos-examples
do.call(rbind, lapply(
  c("Noun", "Verb", "Adjective"),
  function(level) major_pos[which(major_pos$part_of_speech == level)[[1L]], c(
    "item", "part_of_speech", "mean_log_rt", "frequency_subtlex",
    "duration_ms", "n_phones"
  )]
))
```

These SUBTLEX-derived labels summarize a word form's dominant category. Token level syntactic analyses in sentences are unavailable in this dataset.

The fitted contrast between verbs and nouns is `r sprintf("%.4f", coef(fit)[["part_of_speech2"]])` log response time units at the same modeled numeric predictors. The contrast between adjectives and nouns is `r sprintf("%.4f", coef(fit)[["part_of_speech3"]])`.

```{r}
#| label: plot-mald-treatment-coding
#| fig-cap: "Observed MALD item summaries and adjusted part-of-speech means at observed mean frequency, duration, and phone count."
prediction_data <- data.frame(
  part_of_speech = factor(
    levels(major_pos$part_of_speech),
    levels = levels(major_pos$part_of_speech)
  ),
  log_frequency_c = 0,
  log_duration_c = 0,
  n_phones_c = 0
)
interval <- predict(fit, newdata = prediction_data, interval = "confidence")
prediction_data$fit <- interval[, "fit"]
prediction_data$low <- interval[, "lwr"]
prediction_data$high <- interval[, "upr"]

point_opacity <- 0.08
ggplot(major_pos, aes(part_of_speech, mean_log_rt)) +
  geom_jitter(color = "grey70", alpha = point_opacity, width = 0.16, height = 0, size = 0.6) +
  geom_pointrange(
    data = prediction_data,
    aes(y = fit, ymin = low, ymax = high),
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Frequency-dominant part of speech",
    y = "Mean log lexical-decision time"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

Changing the reference category changes the coefficient labels, not the fitted value for any item. [Sum coding](sum-coding.qmd) demonstrates this invariance with a different basis.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. What does the intercept represent under noun-reference coding?
2. Which categories does the verb coefficient compare?
3. Why is the category variable not intrinsically numeric?
4. Which quantities should remain unchanged under recoding?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Under noun-reference coding, the intercept is the fitted noun mean at mean log frequency, mean log duration, and mean phone count. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The verb coefficient compares the fitted verb mean with the fitted noun mean at the same numeric predictor values. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The category variable's labels define groups but provide no intrinsic spacing, order, or arithmetic operation; those properties must come from declared contrasts. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Fitted values, residuals, SSE, and predictions for the same observed conditions should remain unchanged under full-rank recoding. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

We next change the coefficient basis with [sum coding](sum-coding.qmd) while preserving the fitted category means.
